title: WHY DID JESUS CALL THE BLEEDING WOMAN “DAUGHTER”?
paragraphs: WHY DID JESUS CALL THE BLEEDING WOMAN “DAUGHTER”?
She came looking for a healing. Jesus stopped the entire crowd because He wanted to give her something even deeper: a name she may have forgotten she still had.
There is one word in Mark 5 that is dangerously easy to read too quickly.
Jesus could have simply said, “You are healed.”
He could have allowed the woman to disappear back into the crowd with her miracle.
After all, wasn’t that what she came for?
Twelve years of reaching for answers and watching hope disappear.
Why did He bring a frightened, trembling woman out of hiding?
And when she finally fell before Him and told Him “all the truth,” why did Jesus look at this woman and call her something extraordinarily tender?
Not even “the woman who was healed.”
And perhaps that single word was part of the miracle.
Mark records the words of Jesus in Greek:
“Θυγάτηρ, ἡ πίστις σου σέσωκέν σε· ὕπαγε εἰς εἰρήνην…”
Thygatēr, hē pistis sou sesōken se; hypage eis eirēnēn…
“Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace…” — Mark 5:34
Because before Jesus called her “daughter,” Mark never gives us her name.
We know that Jairus was a ruler of the synagogue.
We know Jairus had a daughter.
Mark introduces her simply as “a certain woman” who had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years.
Try to feel the weight of that before turning it into a Sunday-school story.
This was not a bad week.
Not three months of unanswered prayer.
Life continued around her while her own body remained trapped in a nightmare that would not end.
Mark tells us that she had suffered many things from many physicians and had spent everything she possessed. Instead of improving, she became worse.
Imagine spending your money because you desperately want your old life back.
Until eventually the money is disappearing almost as relentlessly as the blood.
And perhaps you understand her better than you thought.
Maybe you have never bled for twelve years.
But you know what it means to carry something for so long that you stop remembering who you were before it began.
A secret sin nobody knows about.
A prayer you have prayed so many times that you are almost embarrassed to pray it again.
Depression behind a smiling Facebook photograph.
A betrayal you supposedly “got over” years ago.
A past you cannot forgive yourself for.
You can become so accustomed to pain that eventually pain starts introducing you.
And if you hear those names long enough, eventually you can start calling yourself by them too.
Because this story is about far more than blood.

According to Leviticus 15:25–27, an ongoing discharge of blood placed a woman in a state of ritual uncleanness under Israel’s covenant law. Objects on which she lay or sat were affected by that uncleanness, and those who touched such things became ceremonially unclean until evening and underwent the prescribed washing.
That needs to be understood carefully.
Ritual uncleanness was not the same thing as personal moral guilt.
The Bible does not say this woman was bleeding because she was especially sinful.
It does not tell us she was being punished for some secret wickedness.
Scripture gives us no permission to invent that accusation.
But her condition had profound religious and social consequences.
And it had lasted twelve years.
And somewhere inside that mass of humanity is a woman who knows what her condition means.
She does not walk toward Jesus demanding attention.
“If I may touch but his clothes,” she tells herself, “I shall be whole.”
There is something painfully human about that sentence.
She does not appear to be looking for a conversation.
She does not ask for the crowd to make room.
She does not request a microphone.
She does not announce twelve years of suffering.
She just wants to touch Him and disappear.
Maybe suffering taught her to survive without being noticed.
Maybe shame taught her to keep her head down.
Maybe disappointment taught her not to expect too much.
But faith whispered one more time:
Imagine the second she realized it.
Something inside her body was different.
The thing doctors could not stop had stopped.
The thing money could not fix had been fixed.
The thing twelve years could not change changed in a moment in the presence of Christ.
People are pressing against You everywhere.
But Jesus knew this touch was different.
One woman had reached for Him in faith.
This is where the story becomes uncomfortable.
Mark says she came “fearing and trembling.”
Then she fell down before Him.
Those words deserve to sit in the room for a while.
Because many of us want Jesus to heal what hurts without exposing what we hide.
We want to touch His garment and quietly return to the shadows.
But sometimes Jesus loves us too deeply to leave us healed and hiding.
So she tells Him the truth.
The woman the narrative has left unnamed is personally addressed by Jesus with a family word.
And Mark 5 contains a breathtaking narrative contrast.
Jesus is already on His way to help somebody else’s daughter.
Jairus has begged Jesus because his little girl is dying.
Mark tells us that Jairus’s daughter is twelve years old.
And the suffering woman has been bleeding for twelve years.
One has apparently spent twelve years growing up.
The other has spent twelve years bleeding.
One is known as the daughter of an important man.
The other woman’s father is not mentioned at all.
One has someone publicly pleading for her.
The other has apparently come alone.
Because the desperate woman in the crowd is not invisible to Him.
And suddenly Jesus says to this woman:
She came secretly seeking power from Jesus.
Jesus allowed her to stand before the crowd no longer merely as the woman with the bleeding, but as someone publicly addressed with tenderness.
This is not sentimental decoration added to the miracle.
Jesus could have spoken without that word.
And there is no need to exaggerate the passage to feel its force.

The crucial verb is σέσωκέν — sesōken, from σῴζω — sōzō, a word whose semantic range can include saving, rescuing, delivering, and making well depending on context. Here the woman has unquestionably experienced physical healing, and Jesus explicitly confirms it. The language is rich enough that English translations variously communicate the idea of being healed, made well, or made whole.
She was not healed because she discovered a spiritual technique.
Jesus was the object of her faith.
Biblical faith is not confidence in confidence.
It is not positive thinking with religious vocabulary.
That distinction matters because somebody reading this has been blaming yourself for not having enough faith.
Someone told you that if your faith were stronger, the disease would disappear.
Please do not turn this woman’s story into a weapon against suffering Christians.
Mark 5 does not teach that every faithful Christian will receive immediate physical healing in this present life if only they believe intensely enough.
Paul prayed about his thorn and received sustaining grace rather than the removal he requested.
Faithful believers still die awaiting the resurrection.
Christian hope is not that believers can force God to perform the miracle they choose.
Christian hope is that Jesus Christ can be trusted even when we cannot dictate what He does.
And ultimately every person who belongs to Christ will experience a healing more complete than anything medicine can accomplish—the resurrection of the body and life with Him.
But this woman’s healing was real.
Jesus wanted her to know who had healed her.
And perhaps He wanted the crowd to know too.
She would not have to spend tomorrow wondering whether the miracle might disappear because she had stolen something from Jesus.
She had not stolen a miracle.
You can have a changed circumstance and still possess a terrified heart.
You can escape the scandal and still live expecting somebody to expose you.
You can receive forgiveness and continue punishing yourself.
You can walk out of the prison while the prison keeps living inside your mind.
Jesus did not merely address what was leaving her body.
He spoke to the woman who would have to live after the miracle.
And maybe that is why this story found you today.
Because perhaps you have spent years believing the worst thing that happened to you became your name.
Maybe somebody labeled you by your darkest chapter.
You walk into church carrying names Jesus never gave you.
You worship while remembering what you did.
You raise your hands while wondering whether God remembers where those hands have been.
You hear people talk about grace, but somewhere inside you still believe grace is beautiful for everybody except you.
Jesus did not come for people who successfully cleaned themselves before approaching Him.
He ate with tax collectors and sinners.
He confronted sin without surrendering sinners to hopelessness.
And eventually He walked toward a cross carrying something infinitely more devastating than ceremonial uncleanness.
“He was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities…” — Isaiah 53:5.
At Calvary, Jesus did not merely risk His reputation by standing near sinners.
The sinless Son of God was crucified.
And the One who called this suffering woman “daughter” made the way for rebellious sons and daughters to be reconciled to God through His death and resurrection.
Not that your past was imaginary.
Not that sin does not matter.
Not that everything you did was secretly okay.
Your sin is serious enough that Christ had to die—and His grace is powerful enough that Christ willingly died to save sinners who could never save themselves.
Repentance does not mean pretending the scandal never happened.
Grace means the scandal no longer gets the final word.
That is why Gospel Warrior keeps returning to this truth:
The Samaritan woman really had a complicated history.
The thief really hung on a cross because he was guilty.
Grace does not require us to lie about the chapter.
Grace changes who writes the ending.
And maybe you have been trying to disappear into the crowd.
Touching the edges of Christian community.
Jesus is not calling you out to humiliate you.
He calls sinners out of darkness because grace gives us somewhere better to live.
“Jesus, I don't know whether I can keep fighting.”
There is no confession you can make that surprises the Christ who already knew what He was carrying when He went to Calvary.
Or simply write, “Jesus, have mercy on me.”
Not because typing words earns salvation.
But sometimes a small public confession becomes the moment we stop protecting the mask.
Someone reading the comments may need to discover they are not fighting alone.
If you need prayer, say it plainly:
And if Christ has already brought you through a chapter you thought would destroy you, tell somebody what He did.
Your testimony may become another wounded person's reason to reach toward Jesus tonight.
Then think of one person who needs this story.
The friend who has been unusually quiet.
The brother who stopped attending church.
The woman carrying a divorce she thinks disqualified her forever.
The person who thinks Christians would reject them if everyone knew the truth.
For somebody else, those seconds could place Scripture in front of them at exactly the moment they were preparing to give up.
There may come a night when shame starts calling you by your old name again.
Remember the Christ who stops for trembling people.
Remember that the crowd does not determine your worth.
Remember that your suffering does not get to rename you.
Remember that forgiveness is not purchased by your perfection.

And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you grow closer to Jesus, confront sin, understand Scripture, return to prayer, and remember the Gospel when life becomes dark, consider staying close to this ministry.
And the New Testament describes Christian giving as willing rather than coerced: “not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
For Christians who practice tithing through their local church, continue honoring your biblical convictions and responsibilities there.
If financial support is not possible for you, please never believe you are less valuable here.
Those acts can help Gospel truth travel far beyond what one ministry could accomplish alone.
Do it as worshipful generosity if God has genuinely placed it on your heart—not from guilt, fear, pressure, or the belief that you can purchase God's approval.
Because God does not need your money.
But Gospel ministry in this world is carried forward through ordinary believers who pray, give, serve, speak, share, sacrifice, encourage, and refuse to keep the good news to themselves.
The woman in Mark 5 thought she was reaching through a crowd for one final chance.
She did not know that millions of people would still be talking about that moment centuries later.
She thought she needed only healing.
And perhaps the most painful thing about your life right now is not simply what happened to you.
Perhaps it is what you started calling yourself because of it.
At the intersection of desperation and faith.
Where grace becomes more than a theological word.
Where wounded people discover that Christ is not frightened by their wounds.
Come after everybody else gave up on you.
Because Christianity is not ultimately the story of wounded people learning to repair themselves.
It is the story of sinners who could not save themselves being rescued by a crucified and risen Savior.
And when grace finally reaches the chapter you were certain had ruined the whole story, you may discover something breathtaking:
Jesus never needed your worst chapter erased before He could begin writing redemption across it.
Because somewhere tonight, another trembling person is hiding in another crowd, believing nobody sees the blood, nobody knows the shame, and nobody remembers their name.
But Jesus has never confused your wound with your name.
